analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans legally import cheaper FDA-approved prescription drugs from other countries.
analysis.headline: The bill sat on the Senate calendar for over ten months and never came up for a vote before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Health and Human Services Secretary to write rules letting ordinary individuals, not just pharmacists and wholesalers, import prescription drugs approved by the FDA from abroad, where prices are often much lower. It also would have made the importation program permanent by removing its sunset date and required counterfeit-resistant packaging, similar to security features on U.S. currency, on prescription drugs. The bill's own findings state Americans pay the highest drug prices in the world, in some cases up to 1,000 percent more than consumers elsewhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially seniors who buy brand-name drugs, would gain the ability to buy FDA-approved medicines from foreign markets at prices far below U.S. prices. Removing the sunset date would make those savings permanent rather than a short-term experiment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans paying high prescription drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have let 'qualifying individuals' — ordinary people, not just pharmacists and wholesalers — import covered drug products under regulations the HHS Secretary must issue, expanding on what current law allows.
It would have struck the sunset date in existing importation law, making the importation provisions permanent instead of temporary.

The bill's findings state that Americans pay up to 1,000 percent more to fill prescriptions than consumers in other countries, and that the U.S. is the largest pharmaceutical market in the world yet pays the highest prices.

It would have required counterfeit-resistant packaging on prescription drugs — visible security technologies similar to those the Bureau of Engraving and Printing uses on currency — with a chain-of-custody labeling system so shipments could be verified as authentic.

The bill would have required importers to conduct authenticity and degradation testing of imported products, and removed the Secretary's ability to block importation by deciding the public is not adequately protected.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers bear the main cost: cheaper parallel imports would erode the premium prices American consumers currently pay, which the industry says funds research and development. Drug makers would also face compliance costs to add the mandated counterfeit-resistant packaging.

drawbacks.text: The bill weakens some safety checks for personal imports: the CRS summary notes that authenticity and degradation tests would not be required unless the importer is a wholesaler, and the Secretary would not have to store records for products imported by qualifying individuals.

Opponents of drug importation have long argued that a looser import channel raises the risk of counterfeit or substandard medicines reaching American patients; the bill tries to answer that with mandatory counterfeit-resistant packaging and importer testing, but those safeguards impose real compliance costs on manufacturers and cannot eliminate the risk entirely.

Lower U.S. drug prices from reimportation would reduce pharmaceutical company revenue, which the industry argues would mean less money for developing new medicines — a cost an honest supporter of the bill would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit for consumers is large: access to the same FDA-approved drugs at foreign prices, made permanent. The main costs are reduced pharmaceutical revenues (which the industry links to research funding) and somewhat weaker record-keeping and testing requirements for personal imports, partially offset by strict counterfeit-resistant packaging rules. The trade-off is real but weighs heavily toward consumers; the deeper problem is that the bill never got a chance to be debated or amended on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late February 2004 and placed on the Senate calendar, but Senate leaders never scheduled it for debate or a vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan introduced the bill on February 26, 2004, joined by Senators Snowe, Stabenow, McCain, and Daschle — a bipartisan group of four cosponsors.
After being read twice, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on February 27, 2004, as Calendar No. 436 — meaning it was waiting to be called up for debate.
The only action for the next six months was sponsor introductory remarks on September 8, 2004; the bill was never debated or voted on, and no House action is recorded.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill died on the calendar without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: with the bill never reaching a vote, the U.S. remained a market where American consumers pay higher prices than patients abroad, and the companies kept the revenue that comes with that. Consumers who needed cheaper medicines gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.role: Senator from North Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave floor remarks on it in September 2004, arguing Americans pay far more for prescriptions than consumers elsewhere.

for.name: Sens. Olympia Snowe and John McCain
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the reimportation bill as its two Republican supporters.

for.name: Sens. Debbie Stabenow and Tom Daschle
for.role: Democratic cosponsors (Daschle was Senate Minority Leader)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the reimportation bill as its two Democratic supporters.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled the Senate floor schedule in the 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never called the bill up from the calendar for debate or a vote during the roughly ten months it sat there.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturer lobby
against.role: Industry trade groups representing brand-name drug makers
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained campaign against drug reimportation legislation, arguing it would jeopardize drug safety and undermine research funding.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — two Republicans and two Democrats joined the Democratic sponsor — but the bill never got a roll-call vote, so the chamber's full partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: Reimportation would have let Americans buy the same FDA-approved drugs at the lower prices charged abroad, directly cutting into the premium prices U.S. patients pay. The bill's own findings state Americans pay the highest drug prices in the world.
As authorized importers alongside wholesalers and pharmacists, licensed pharmacies could have built a legal importation business passing foreign price savings to consumers.

industries.industry: Anti-counterfeiting packaging and security technology vendors
industries.note: The bill mandates currency-style counterfeit-resistant packaging on all prescription drugs, creating a new compliance market for security printing technology.
